en: The *Śramaṇa Ji* composed this commentary on the scripture, from "All World-Honored Ones" up to "the Single and Unique Vehicle. The eulogy states:
The fifth section below consists of seventy and a half verses; these verses explain the fifth [topic], the reliance upon the Dharma, which has three parts, the first of which is as follows:

The first thirty-eight and a half verses praise the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions; the next thirty-eight and a half verses praise the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time; and the final thirty and a half verses praise that "I, too, am likewise."
This is the first [point].
Since there is only the One Vehicle and no second vehicle, how is it that the three are refuted in order to return to the one?
The Sūtra says: "From incalculable past kalpas until their number becomes immeasurable."
The commentary states:
The final thirty-eight and a half verses praise the three periods of time, divided into three sections:
first, twenty-seven and a half verses praise the past; second, six and a half verses praise the future; and third, four and a half verses praise the present.
The beginning and middle [of this section] consist of two parts:

first, four and a half verses praise the Buddha’s teaching of the provisional at the outset and the ultimate at the end; second, twenty-three verses praise how sentient beings who hear the Dharma all ultimately attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The beginning and middle [of this section] consist of four parts:

first, one verse on the abundance of Buddhas; second, one verse on the revelation of the provisional (opening the power); third, one verse on the manifestation of the real; and fourth, one and a half verses explaining the intent behind revealing the real through the opening of the provisional.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the sūtra passage from “In this way, all those World-Honored Ones” to “expounding the characteristics of all dharmas,” the commentary says:
The *Mingchu kaiquan* [Exposition on the Opening of the Provisional at the Beginning of the Ming] quotes the scripture: “These World-Honored Ones... lead them to enter the Buddha-way.
It comments:
This clarifies the provisional and reveals the ultimate.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Furthermore, all the Great Holy Lords" to "assisting in the revelation of the primary meaning," the commentary states:
This explains the meaning of "expounding the provisional to reveal the real.

Because [the Buddha] knows that sentient beings are unable to study the teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) all at once, and because he recognizes their faculties and inclinations, he first employs provisional skillful means (*upāya*) to assist in revealing the One Vehicle, and subsequently causes them to enter the reality.
Furthermore, there are two types of bodhisattva faculties and natures:
first, the indeterminate nature; second, the determinate nature.
For those of indeterminate nature, the provisional comes first and the real follows later, thereby fully manifesting the One Vehicle; this is what is indicated by the preceding two verses.
For those of fixed nature, the Sudden Teaching of the One Vehicle is expounded; this text is precisely that.

It means that because one knows the minds and natures of sentient beings desire [enlightenment] all at once, one employs diverse skillful means—not following the provisional to grasp the real, but manifesting as an aid to the One Vehicle. The "One Vehicle" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), *tathatā*, and so forth.
The first three chapters and the final one constitute the provisional and ultimate skillful means; because they expound the One Vehicle all at once, they are termed "extraordinary skillful means.
This refers to the passage in the sutra: "If there are any classes of sentient beings... [omitted] ...all have already attained the path of Buddhahood."
The commentary states:
The following twenty-three verses show that sentient beings who hear the Dharma ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is divided into three parts:
the first two verses concern the Buddha’s presence; the next twenty verses concern the period after his parinirvāṇa; and the final verse provides the conclusion.
This is the first [category].

Those who encountered the Buddhas, heard the Dharma, and practiced the six perfections, the four means of attraction, and the immeasurable [dharmas] are called "various merits. Because they cultivated the causes for Buddhahood through the practices of a bodhisattva, they have all already attained the Way.
Regarding the passage from "After the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa" to "have all already attained the Buddha-way," the commentary states:
The following twenty verses concern the period after the Buddhas' passing and are divided into five sections.

One verse on the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), four and a half verses on constructing stūpas, six and a half verses on constructing images, seven verses on making offerings, and one verse on praising the Buddha— this is the first section.

There are those who are virtuous yet rigid, who are not Bodhisattvas; there are those whose minds are supple yet lack virtue, who are likewise neither virtuous nor Bodhisattvas. It is only when one is both virtuous and supple that it constitutes the mind of a Bodhisattva, for such a mind accords with principle, benefits all beings, and is supremely gentle and harmonious.
"Having already attained the Buddha-way" refers to having planted the causes for Buddhahood.
The subsequent passages are based on practices performed after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa because they are difficult to perform and constitute distinct practices;
it is not that these various practices were performed while the Buddha was still present and yet were not causes for Buddhahood, for those [practices] are easy to cultivate.
Following the above, practicing the six perfections after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa constitutes comprehensive practice, and thus one also attains the Buddha-way.
As the Sūtra says: "After all Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, [one] proceeds to adorn their various stūpas."
The commentary states:
The following four and a half verses concern the construction of stupas and the attainment of Buddhahood, which is divided into two parts:
the first four verses clarify the construction of the stupas, and the latter half of the verse provides the conclusion.

The initial section consists of three parts: the first two verses describe the construction of numerous stupas adorned with the eight precious treasures; the next verse describes stupas made of nine types of materials; and the final verse extends down to stupas made of inferior objects used even in jest.
This is the first point.

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* enumerates the seven treasures without including *mrgaśṛṅga* (amber/coral), and it distinguishes between *vaidūrya* (lapis lazuli) and *maṇi* (jewel); here, "jewel" refers to red pearls (*lohitamuktikā*).
If one were to take *vaidūrya* as the "jewel," there would then be seven treasures; otherwise, there are eight, because *vaidūrya* and the "jewel" are distinct.

Spinel (*sphaṭika*) is white with a reddish tint; musaragalva is a variegated color of blue and white; agate has many colors—sometimes pure white, sometimes pure blue or yellow, or variegated with various hues; and coral is red.
The *Shuowen* states: "A fire-aligned pearl.
One explanation says that among stones, those of exquisite beauty are called *mei*, and those that are round and beautiful are called *gui*; other types may be inferred from this.
In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I shall now declare the four merits of the Brahmā realm:

first, if faithful sons of good family and others erect a stūpa where none has previously been raised; second, to repair and maintain old monasteries; third, to bring the noble Saṃgha into harmony; fourth, when the Buddha has first attained the Way, to entreat him to turn the wheel of Dharma. These are called the four merits of the Brahmā realm."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"How much is the merit of Brahma-merit?
The Buddha said:

The merit possessed by all beings in the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm is still not equal to the merit of a single Brahmā king; therefore, it is exhorted that by constructing a stūpa, one shall attain bodhi.
The Sūtra states: "There are some who erect stone shrines, up to those made of brick, tile, mud, and earth.
The Commentary says:
This single verse refers to nine types of materials for constructing a stūpa.

"Stone Temple" refers to a stone Buddha hall; anciently called a *caitya* (zhiti), now called a *caitya* (zhidu), translated as a "spiritual temple. It should be written with the character for "temple" (miào), meaning its sacred appearance.
The *Baihutong* and the *Yupian* state: "Because it is the place where the honored appearance of the ancestors resides, it is called a temple (*miao*).

Regarding "wood *mi*": the *Zilin* calls it "fragrant wood"; the *Qieyun* writes it as "xiá" (榓), while the *Yupian* writes it as "mi" (櫁). This tree resembles the *huái* tree and is extremely fragrant; it must be felled five years before it can be used. If one wishes to extract its fragrance, the wood must first be ground for a long period before the scent emerges.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "If in the midst of a wilderness" down to "all have already attained the Buddha-way," the commentary states:
The first verse, extending down to "making a stūpa out of inferior objects even in jest," concludes with the latter half-verse.

The treatise states: "Regarding the statement that those who pile up sand to form a stupa for the Buddha thereby accomplish the path to Buddhahood, this means that those who have resolved their minds on Bodhi and practice as Bodhisattvas can realize Bodhi through the roots of goodness they perform; it is not something that can be attained by ordinary worldlings, nor by Śrāvakas of fixed lineage who have not yet resolved their minds on Bodhi. This applies likewise to the aforementioned passages and even to minor acts such as bowing one's head."
The Sūtra says: "If a person acts for the sake of the Buddha... all have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
The commentary states:
The following six and a half verses clarify the creation of images; within these, there are two parts.
The first five verses constitute the composition, and the final one and a half verses constitute the conclusion.
Within the initial section, there are four parts:
one verse on carving and sculpting, two verses on adornment with ten types of objects, one verse on colored painting, and one verse on playful craftsmanship.
This is the first point.
It clarifies that one makes an image of the Buddha and not an image of anything else; therefore, it is said to be "for the sake of the Buddha.
Because one acts for the purpose of seeking to become a Buddha and contemplates with reverence for the Buddha, it is called "the Buddha."
Furthermore, it is said that making various images for the sake of the Buddha is called "the Buddha" because they serve to adorn the Buddha.
The *Sūtra on the Merit of Image-Making* states:
"By making an image, one obtains eleven kinds of fruits:"

"First, in every lifetime one will be born with pure eyes and a handsome countenance; second, one will never be born in an evil place; third, one will always be born into a noble family; fourth, one’s body will be beautiful, with the color of purple-polished gold; fifth, one will always abound in rare treasures and playthings; sixth, one will be born into a family of the wise and virtuous; seventh, in a subsequent birth one will become a king, the most excellent among kings; eighth, one will become a golden-wheel-turning monarch; ninth, in a subsequent birth one will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven with a lifespan of one kalpa; tenth, one will not follow the evil paths; eleventh, in subsequent births one will again revere the Triple Gem, delight in upholding sublime things, and further create merit. The merit of these ten Brahma-merits is ten times greater than the waters of the great oceans of the four continents.
The Sūtra says: "Or [images] made of the seven treasures... all have already attained the Buddha-way.
The commentary states:
These two verses describe the creation of images adorned with ten kinds of materials.
The *Qieyun* states: "Lead (yán) is the same as tin (xī).
Some say: "Tin is between silver and lead. The *Yupian* defines it as: "A blue metal."
The Sūtra states: "From painting images of the Buddha with colored pigments... until all have attained the Way of the Buddha.
The commentary says:
This praises the painting of Buddhas.
The Sūtra says: "Even down to children playing, they draw images of the Buddha.
The commentary states:
This verse concerns playful imitation.
The Sūtra says: "In this way, these people and others... until they have delivered immeasurable multitudes.
The Commentary states:
This is the conclusion.

Regarding "endowed with a heart of great compassion": whatever good deeds one performs must necessarily be accompanied by compassion in order to reach the other shore and thereby attain the Buddha-way.
As the Sūtra says: "If a person, at a stupa or temple, makes offerings with a heart of supreme reverence..."
The commentary states:
Below are seven verses clarifying the offerings, which are divided into two parts:
the first five and a half verses clarify the offerings, and the final one and a half verses provide the conclusion.
The beginning consists of five parts:

one verse on the offering of four types of material objects; one and a half verses on the offering of music and dance; one verse on the offering of chanted hymns; one verse on the offering of flowers; and one verse on the offering of reverent service through physical action.
This is the first. The *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* states:
"If one offers flowers, one attains the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment."
By giving incense as an offering, one attains the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body;
by giving banners as an offering, one attains dhāraṇīs that transform all evils;
by giving canopies as an offering, one obtains the four immeasurables to shelter all sentient beings.
The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states that each [of these acts] attains ten virtues.
Regarding the passage in the sutra: "If one causes others to perform music, up to the point of making offerings with their entire possessions," the commentary says:

This refers to making offerings with music. The character for "music" (*lè*) is pronounced with the *wǔ* and *jué* finals; it is so called because it generates joy (*lè*), and it is also pronounced with the *lù* and *yù* finals. During the era of the Yellow Emperor, Ling Lun created music. According to the *Shuowen*, it is the general name for the five tones and eight musical instruments; according to the *Liji*, that which consists of shields, axes, feathers, and plumes is called "music."
Zheng Xuan said: "When the eight musical instruments are in perfect harmony, it is called music (yue).
'Gong' (drum) means to move or to sound; generally, anything that produces sound is called a drum. Now, when wood covered with skin is struck, it immediately sounds."
"Jiǎo" (Horn) refers to a curved shape resembling a horn.
"Bèi" (Conch) refers to a spiral shell; as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, one blows the conch to signal the time.
"Xiāo" (Flute) refers to a pipe; according to the *Yùpiān*, it is "blown by weaving small tubes together," and it is also called a *shuāo*.

"Flute" (*dì*): A seven-holed *yè*; commonly known as the *zhí*. According to the *Yùpiān*, "The bamboo flute has five holes; the Qiang flute has three. "Zither" (*qín*): It means "to restrain" (*jìn*).
The gentleman restrains himself by adhering to correctness; it was created by Shennong.
The *konghou* and *pipa* can be understood by comparison.
The *niao* is like a bell but larger; according to the *Yupian*, it is a "small *zheng*.

According to military law, the leader of ten men holds the *niao*. Five men form a *wu*; five *wu*s, or twenty-five men, form a *liang*, and the *liang-sima* (commander of two) holds the *duo* (gong).
Copper *paṭaha* drums consist of two halves that strike against each other to produce sound; there is no source for the reading "bō" (cymbals), though some take it as the character "bá.
The *Bodhicittotpāda Sūtra* states:

"One should not give music or female forms as gifts, for they disturb sentient beings. This does not contradict [the practice of offering such things], because these are offered to the Buddha, as seen in the accounts of musical offerings in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.
The Sūtra says: "Or with a heart of joy... all have already attained the Way of the Buddha.
The commentary states:
This refers to making offerings through song and chant, for by doing so one shall attain the Brahma-voice of a Mahāsattva.
In Sanskrit it is called *vādita*, which here means "praise"; "bai ni" (唄匿) is a corruption of this term.

When Chen Si climbed Mount Yushan and heard the chanting of sutras from within a mountain cave, its purity, elegance, vigor, and resonance echoed through the distant valleys. He subsequently modeled his compositions upon that sound to create *fanbai* (Brahmanic chants); thus, they are colloquially referred to as "Yushan Brahmans. This was a profound convergence with the three rhythms and seven tones employed by the *śrāvakas* such as Kūṭadanta in the Western Regions.
The Sūtra says: "If a person, with a distracted mind... gradually sees countless Buddhas.
The Commentary states:
This refers to making offerings with flowers.
How does this differ from the four previous matters concerning giving in China?
Those were performed with a focused mind of goodness, whereas this is done with a distracted mind; therefore, they do not contradict one another.
To speak briefly, while making offerings to painted images is specifically mentioned, it is also permissible to make offerings to other types of images.
The Sūtra says: "There may be some who prostrate themselves, or even those who slightly bow their heads.
The Commentary states:
This clarifies the performance of reverent offerings through the action of the body (*kāyakarman*).
The chanting of hymns above is the karma of speech;
the ability to give rise to the thought of enlightenment is the karma of mind; all else constitutes external material offerings and the practice of offerings through the three karmas.
The Sūtra says: "With this, one makes offerings to the image until it is like fire being extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
The commentary states:
This concludes the section on making offerings.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "If a person with a distracted mind... up to "...have all already attained the Buddha-way," the commentary states:
This refers to reciting the name of the Buddha to become a Buddha; if even a single recitation can lead one to Buddhahood, how much more so many recitations?

As it is said in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-sūtra*: "Because I have constantly recited the names of the fifty-three Buddhas, I have now attained Buddhahood. This refers precisely to that matter.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, "In all past Buddhas... until they have all already attained the Buddha-way," the commentary states:
Within the verses on sentient beings hearing the Dharma and attaining the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), this constitutes the third point: the consummation of the Buddha-way.
Regarding the sūtra passage, “The future World-Honored Ones will likewise teach the Dharma through skillful means,” the commentary states:
The following six and a half verses concern the Dharma of the future, which is divided into two parts.
The first three and a half verses establish that the teaching here is identical to the teaching on reality; the subsequent three verses re-explain the meaning of the former.
Within the former section, there are three parts:

one verse establishes the identity with the initial expedient means; one and a half verses establish the subsequent accomplishment of the teaching on reality; and one verse explains the reason for the former.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the Sūtra passage: "All Tathāgatas, down to those who have not yet attained Buddhahood," the commentary says:

This verse indicates that what follows is the explanation of the ultimate truth, enabling all who hear the Dharma to attain Buddhahood; thus, both the Buddhas and sentient beings are discussed together.
This corresponds to the passage in the Sūtra from "The original vows of all Buddhas" to "shall likewise attain this Way."
The commentary states:
To explain the reason for what preceded, it is because of his original vow.
This is as the Sūtra says: "From the Buddhas of future ages... down to its ultimate realization, it is but the One Vehicle."
The commentary states:
The following three verses re-explain the preceding meaning in two parts:

the first verse clarifies that the initial expedient means are all for the sake of the One Vehicle; the latter two verses clarify why the realization of the three natures leads all dharmas to this ultimate destination.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the scriptural passage from “The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among Two-legged Beings” to “the Guide’s skillful means,” the commentary says:
He clearly realizes that all phenomena of the three natures converge toward this destination; therefore, he first employs expedient means and later teaches the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The wondrous principle of *tathatā* is eternally abiding in its essential nature, which the Buddha is able to realize and know. The two kinds of self—the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dharma-self—are non-existent in their essential nature; because the Buddha has realized the principle of selflessness, he also knows that this non-existence is what ordinary beings falsely and delusively cling to.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha-seed arises from conditions": the seeds of the *nirmāṇakāya* (retribution-Buddha) based upon the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) *paratantra* arise from conditions and originate through conditions, because they are produced by cultivation.

Because one realizes the ultimate truth and thereby abandons the afflicted portion of the dependent nature—the mind that grasps—and knows that the grasped object does not exist, those who cultivate the seeds of Buddhahood based on the pure portion of the dependent nature do so by way of the Single Vehicle.
What is the One Vehicle?

It is the further manifestation of the eternal Dharma, which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the phrase "the Dharma abides in its own place" (*dharmasthititā*): True Suchness (*tathatā*) dwells within all phenomena; because its essential nature is eternally present, it is called the "abiding of the Dharma."
Dharmas possess both defilement and purity; because the state of attaining purity by departing from defilement is manifested therein, it is called the "dharma-position" (*dharmapada*).

As for "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the essential nature (*svabhāva*); the fundamental substance of the world is precisely the eternally abiding true suchness (*tathatā*) and reality-essence, which is the essence of the One Vehicle.

Within the Vajrāsana maṇḍala, having realized the fundamental nature of these phenomena, the Teacher employs skillful means to describe them through names and signs within the realm of nameless and signless phenomena. Briefly stated, among all phenomena there are two kinds:
first, emptiness; second, existence.
Emptiness, being without differentiation, is collectively established as a single nature, termed "the existence of the thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Phenomena (*dharma*), however, possess differentiation and are divided into two:
first, the permanent; second, the impermanent.
The permanent is termed the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); the impermanent is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The dependent nature is further divided into two:
first, the contaminated (*sāsrava*), and second, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Here, we rely on the former category.

Impermanence is the dependent [nature]; all dependent phenomena with outflows are completely severed and abandoned. Within this context, we take only the pure portion of the dependent nature that is impermanent and without outflows, because it constitutes the attainment of *bodhi* at the stage of ultimate fulfillment. Therefore, it is said that "the seed of the Buddha arises from conditions."

This is intended to reveal that because one can realize the principle of the eternally abiding *dharmatā-tathatā* (true suchness) and selflessness, one is then able to understand that the two kinds of self do not exist. By relying on spiritual friends and cultivating wisdom, one fulfills the awakening of *bodhi* through dependently originated phenomena. This is for the purpose of realizing the wondrous principle of the One Vehicle’s *tathatā*; this wondrous principle is precisely the abiding nature of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti*), the world’s eternally abiding characteristic.

Having already realized and known the Great Parinirvāṇa within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he now teaches it through skillful means for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may aspire toward and realize it. Here, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is itself bodhi, and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is itself nirvāṇa; these are thus unified as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Because the perfected nature is supreme, it alone is designated as the "One Vehicle."
By severing the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) that is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), one eliminates the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) and realizes these two fruits.

Because one understands both the dependent and the imagined natures, the *Āgama* is taught first and the *Prajñā* is taught next; these teachings of pure existence and emptiness are termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Now, because these three are explained together, it is called "the reality" (*tattva*).
The meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) is as explained in a separate chapter.
The Sūtra says: "Worshipped by gods and humans... [omitted] ...and likewise teaches this Dharma."
The commentary states:
Below are four and a half verses concerning the present; these consist of three parts:
first, one and a half verses as a heading; second, one verse to reveal the provisional and manifest the real; and third, two verses to clarify the underlying intent.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the sūtra passage from "knowing the foremost quiescence" to "its reality is the One Vehicle," the commentary says:
This first section opens up the provisional (upāya), while the latter reveals the ultimate reality (bhūtārtha).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra: "Knowing the various practices of sentient beings, he teaches through appropriate expedient means," the commentary says:
This reveals the meaning that the former is provisional and the latter is ultimate.
"The various activities of sentient beings" is the general statement, referring to the characteristics of mental activity.
The following are the specific statements, which may also refer to resolute belief (*adhimukti*).
"Mindfulness of what is contemplated" refers to the practice leading to all destinations.
"Karmic power" refers to one's own karma.
"Power of desire" refers to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
"Power of nature" (*dhātubala*) refers to the various elements (*dhātu*).
"Power of diligence" (*vīryabala*) refers to the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), and so forth.

Alternatively, the essence of diligence and the other [faculties] is itself the power of nature, because the essence of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is identical to the five faculties (*indriya*); thus, the single term "power" (*bala*) below extends upward to encompass the former as well.
Regarding "the sharpness or dullness of the faculties," this refers to the power of superiority or inferiority of the faculties.
Because the Buddha possesses this power of knowledge and is able to know them, he first employs provisional means and later returns to the ultimate truth.

The Buddhas of the past and future do so by awakening to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), while this present Buddha does so by knowing sentient beings; as these aspects mutually reflect and illuminate one another, the preliminary skillful means are explained first, followed by the ultimate truth.
Regarding the sūtra passage from "Now I am also like this" up to "causing all to attain joy," the commentary states:
the final thirty and a half verses explain that "I am also like this" in the same way as Śākyamuni; this middle section is divided into two parts.
The first two verses provide the heading, while the subsequent twenty-eight and a half verses offer a detailed explanation.
This is the former [section].
The first verse concerns the present reality, while the latter verse concerns the past expedient means; both are intended to cause beings to rejoice and gradually enter the Path.
Regarding the passage from “Śāriputra, you should know” to “poverty-stricken and lacking in merit and wisdom,” the commentary states:
The following is an extensive explanation, divided into two parts:

The first twenty-one and a half verses initially employ the skillful means (*upāya*) of the three vehicles to attract and guide [beings]; as the long prose states: "Knowing that sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated attachments, he preaches the Dharma for them through the power of skillful means—using various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions—in accordance with their fundamental natures.
The subsequent seven verses now explain the ultimate truth; as the long prose states: "All this is for the sake of attaining the One Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
This immediately explains the meaning of the provisional [teaching] first and the ultimate [teaching] last.
Regarding the initial section, it is divided into four parts:

the first three and a half verses describe seeing one's place of birth as a perilous difficulty; the next three verses contemplate that rescue is impossible; the following eleven and a half verses request mindfulness and the establishment of provisional means; and the final three and a half verses correctly explain the transformation through the Three Vehicles.
The first part consists of two sections:
the first verse concerns the absence of goodness, and the second and a half verses concern the presence of evil.
This is the former.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* state that the Buddha possesses five eyes:

first, the flesh eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), which is not produced through meditative cultivation; it is composed of the four great elements, being either nurtured (*aupacayika*) or a result of maturation (*vipākaja*), and has pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) as its essential nature.

Second is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): it severs the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samāpattyāvaraṇa*), arises from cultivation, consists solely of the nourished (*aupacayika*), and has as its nature the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) derived from the four great elements.
Third is the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*): it is the wisdom that contemplates phenomena.
The fourth is the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which is the wisdom that contemplates the principle of emptiness.
The fifth is the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*); because the cause has been accumulated and the fruit is perfected, it takes the preceding four as its essence.

Nāgārjuna explains: "Just as the four great rivers flow into the celestial lake and are collectively termed the 'Great Ocean,' so too do these four eyes flow into the fruit of Buddhahood and are collectively termed the 'Buddha-eye.'"
The first two have as their essence form (*rūpa*); the next two have as their essence wisdom (*jñāna*); and the last one pervades both.

Furthermore, it is said that humans and others possess the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), gods and others possess the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), those of the Two Vehicles possess the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), Bodhisattvas possess the Dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), and Buddhas possess the Buddha eye (*buddha-cakṣus*); it is on this basis that the five are taught.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter fourteen, states that there are three eyes:
first, the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which can illuminate and perceive manifest forms without obstruction;
second, the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), which can illuminate both hidden and manifest forms, whether obstructed or unobstructed.
The three wisdom-eyes can illuminate all kinds of phenomena, whether material or non-material.

The essence of the Dharma-eye is the union of wisdom with wisdom, forming a single entity; unlike the physical eye, whose objects may be hidden or manifest, it is therefore omitted from discussion here.
The Buddha-eye is identical to the aforementioned four eyes; however, because this discussion concerns the cause rather than the fruit, it is not mentioned here.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of ten eyes:
first, the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which sees all forms.
Second is the divine eye, which sees death here and rebirth there;
third is the wisdom eye, which perceives the differences in the faculties of all sentient beings;
fourth is the dharma eye, which perceives the ultimate meaning of all phenomena.
The fifth is the Buddha-eye, which perceives the ten powers of a Buddha;
the sixth is the wisdom-eye, which discerns and thoroughly understands all phenomena in their every aspect;
the seventh is the light-eye, which beholds the radiance of all Buddhas.
Eighth is the eye that emerges from birth and death, which sees the dharma of nirvāṇa;
ninth is the unobstructed eye, which sees all dharmas without hindrance;
tenth is the universal eye, which refers to the dharma-gate of seeing the equality of the dharma-realm.
Among the ten, the first is the first among the five, because it perceives all forms;
the second here is the same as the second previously mentioned;
the third, fifth, sixth, seventh, and ninth of these five eyes are the dharma-eye (dharmacakṣus) mentioned previously.

The fourth and eighth of these are the aforementioned eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), because they perceive the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); alternatively, the fourth, eighth, and ninth—these three eyes—are the aforementioned eye of wisdom, as they both perceive principle (*li*).
The tenth, the universal eye (*samanta-cakṣus*), is the aforementioned Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*), because it universally perceives the equality of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-samatā*).
"Observing with the Buddha-eye" means observing with the Buddha-eye among the five eyes;
for among the ten [eyes], the Buddha-eye does not see sentient beings, but rather sees the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).

Sentient beings in the six realms have, since beginningless time, failed to cultivate the two causes of merit and wisdom; they have not yet obtained the seven kinds of noble wealth, nor the seven dharmas of the human and celestial realms—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and skillful means—and thus they lack both merit and wisdom.
Regarding the sutra passage, "Entering the perilous path of birth and death until one is blind and sees nothing," the commentary states:
The following two and a half verses concern evil, which is divided into two parts.

The first one and a half verses show how beings are submerged in suffering as their afflictions increase; the final verse shows that even if they seek the essential means of liberation, they engage in wrong conduct.
This is the first [point].
Just as a wild ox, out of love for its own tail, hides its body to protect it, yet people, coveting that tail, end up killing its body; so it is with these beings.

Sentient beings are likewise; clinging to the five desires, they conceal themselves within them, and thus, by means of their greedy attachment, they bring about their own ruin, falling instead into self-imposed distress and descending into the evil realms.
Some versions read "self-concealment" (*zì bì*); "concealment" (*bì*) means to cover, obscure, or obstruct.
It is like the yak that loves its tail so much that it uses it to hide its heart, ultimately leading to the loss of its life;
sentient beings are likewise, for craving and attachment conceal their minds.
The *máoniú* (yak): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is "a long-maned ox of the southwestern tribes.
Some write this as the character for "cat" (*māo*), referring to those caught by humans to catch mice; however, that is not the meaning intended here.
Some write "māo" (貓) or "mǎo" (𤚐), not knowing their origin. The scripture says:
"From 'not seeking the Buddha Mahāsthāmaprāpta' up to 'desiring to abandon suffering through suffering.'"

The commentary states: Suppose one seeks the essential path to liberation yet practices deviant conduct; though the Buddha possesses supernatural powers, majestic authority, and the wisdom of the Dharma for severing suffering, one does not seek to follow it, instead falling into the net of heterodox views. To practice various bodily austerities in an attempt to abandon the suffering of birth and death is unacceptable. This is why for six years he consumed only hemp and wheat yet did not realize Bodhi; how could the Way-fruit be attained while sitting or lying upon thorns?
It is like a dog chasing a clod of earth; as the clod rolls away, the dog pursues it further and further. How can this compare to a lion chasing a person rather than a clod?
As the Sūtra says: "For the sake of these sentient beings, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion."
The commentary states:
Regarding the three subsequent verses on the inability to save [sentient beings], they are divided into three parts:
the first half-verse reflects upon the causes and practices; one verse reflects upon the state after attaining the fruit; and one and a half verses reflect upon the impossibility of saving them.
This is the first [section].
Seeing that sentient beings possess these two conditions, he gives rise to a mind of compassion, resolves to practice, and contemplates how to save them.
This is as stated in the Sūtra: "From the time I first sat at the site of enlightenment... until I contemplated such matters."
The commentary states:

Having attained the fruit, he reflected; after the Buddha had completed his enlightenment, he walked back and forth beneath the tree. Observing the tree, he rejoiced that his own path was perfected; as he walked, he contemplated how to benefit sentient beings.
Furthermore, while contemplating the tree, one concentrates the mind on the sublime principle; while walking in meditation, one contemplates transforming all sentient beings.
Furthermore, while contemplating the tree, one envisions it providing shade for the four modes of birth; while walking in meditation, one reflects upon bestowing merit and wisdom.

The various sūtras state that the periods during which the Buddha preached the Dharma after his enlightenment differ from one another; here it is said to be twenty-one days. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there were seven days of samādhi, which is the same as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. He did not preach for seven days in order to manifest his own enjoyment of the bliss of the Dharma, and to cause sentient beings to increase their love and reverence.

According to the Vinaya and the Sarvāstivāda tradition, it was forty-two days—six or seven times seven—before the Dharma was preached, because Brahmā had come to request it and the faculties of Kauṇḍinya and the others had only then matured.
Furthermore, some say that he ordained the five men only after the summer retreat;
the *Dvādaśayojana-sūtra* states that he ordained the five men two years after his enlightenment.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that he did not preach the Dharma for fifty-seven days.
These accounts differ according to various schools and cannot yet be harmonized.

However, those who interpret this today hold that the Mahāyāna takes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as authoritative; since that sūtra speaks of the turning of the wheel of the Four Noble Truths, it refers to the three seven-day periods.

If one speaks only of the turning of the Dharma wheel of the Mahāyāna, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* is authoritative, because the ten stages were taught during the second seven-day period. As the sūtra states:
"The wisdom I have attained... how can it be used to deliver others? and so forth.
The commentary states:
One cannot obtain the means to rescue [sentient beings] due to four causes:

first, the Dharma is profound and difficult to understand; second, their faculties are dull and difficult to save; third, they are attached to pleasure and difficult to detach from; fourth, they are blind with ignorance and difficult to awaken. How, then, can they be delivered?
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "At that time, the various Brahmā kings arrived" to "requesting me to turn the wheel of Dharma," the commentary states:
The following eleven and a half verses request mindfulness and the establishment of skillful means; this middle section is divided into four parts.

The first two verses record the request of the devas for him to preach; the next three verses demonstrate his contemplation of signs; the subsequent four and a half verses describe how he encountered favorable conditions through transformation; and the final two verses reflect upon following expedient inducements.
This is the first [point].
"Maheśvara" refers to a deity of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Now, in contrast to the Three Vehicles, it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that all teachings must await an invitation before being expounded.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven exhorted him to leave the household life; the Four Heavenly Kings offered alms bowls; Śakra offered a precious throne; and Brahmā requested that he turn the wheel of Dharma. The Buddha initially did not consent. When Brahmā explained that there are three faculties [of spiritual capacity] and entreated him with great earnestness, the Buddha finally agreed and first taught the Three Vehicles."
The *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"The Four Heavenly Kings and others offered almsbowls, and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, offered a seat; the Buddha accepted them, yet each perceived that he had received it from himself alone, and all conceived the supreme resolve."

However, while in the *Mahāvaipulya Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa* (Dàtōngzhìshèng) only the Brahmā kings are mentioned as making the request, this present teaching states that it extends to all the devas. That former text cites the most eminent class [of beings], but it is not that other devas did not also request the Buddha.
Regarding the sūtra passage from “I then thought to myself” up to “quickly entering nirvāṇa,” the commentary states:
The following three verses demonstrate the contemplation of characteristics, which is twofold:
The first two verses speak of the Mahāyāna, wherein sentient beings suffer loss;
the final verse speaks provisionally of the Three Vehicles, wherein sentient beings derive benefit.
This is the first [point].

Because sentient beings dwelling in the secular world are currently immersed in suffering, while those who have left the household life engage in the suffering of deluded ascetic practices, they lack the leisure to suddenly believe in the Mahāyāna Dharma; if one were to preach it to them, they would instead give rise to slander, doubt, and destruction, and might even fall into evil realms due to their lack of faith.

Furthermore, those who remain in the secular world do not believe because they are immersed in suffering, and those who have left home as non-Buddhist outsiders do not believe because they subvert the Dharma. Since there is such loss, why would you not preach the Dharma and enter nirvana swiftly? How could you instead cause further harm to all sentient beings?
This is identical to the initial refusal [of the position] in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “Recalling the Buddhas of the past... up to ‘one should also teach the three vehicles’,” the commentary says:
Furthermore, it is said that the Three Vehicles benefit sentient beings because they are identical to all Buddhas.
This is consistent with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states that [the Buddha] granted permission only after repeated requests.
As the Sūtra says: "When he engaged in such reflection, he employed the power of skillful means."
The commentary states:
Following this are four and a half verses. There are three aspects to encountering a favorable condition for transformation:

first, one verse and a half on the Buddha’s manifestation and praise; second, half a verse exhorting others to follow the example of all Buddhas; and third, two and a half verses citing oneself as testimony, wherein the latter is the ultimate truth and the former is the provisional means.
These are the first two [points].

The Buddhas of the ten directions appear and praise the Buddha, exclaiming "Excellent! They laud the Foremost Teacher for attaining the Unsurpassed Dharma, and they urge him to follow the true and provisional teachings of all Buddhas.
Śākya is the clan name; Muni is the title for one who is tranquil. Now, the text is explained briefly according to the phonetic glosses.
It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) to express sympathetic joy, saying, "Excellent!
as the Sūtra states: "We, too, have all attained [the realization that] the three vehicles are taught through differentiation."

The commentary states: The subsequent two and a half verses cite the self as testimony; regarding this, the ultimate is primary while the provisional comes first. Within this section, there are three parts:
the first verse cites the self as testimony; the next verse explains the reason for this; and the final half-verse concludes by returning to the ultimate reality.
This is the first [section].
Having cited the initial teaching of the three vehicles, the Sūtra states:
"Those of little wisdom who delight in the lesser Dharma... [omitted] ...it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas."
The commentary states:

This explains the origin [of the teaching] and concludes by returning to the ultimate truth. Because those of indeterminate capacity initially remain as ordinary beings—possessing limited wisdom, delighting in the small, and lacking aspiration for the Great Meaning—and because they do not believe that they themselves can become Buddhas, the Three Vehicles were taught at first.
Although this was an initial expedient, it must ultimately be the truth; it is simply that [the teaching] transforms bodhisattvas.
Regarding the passage from “Śāriputra, you should know” to “joyfully exclaiming ‘Namo Buddha’,” the commentary states:
The following two verses concern mindfulness that accords with expedient guidance, which is divided into two parts:
One hears the first verse and reverently praises it; one contemplates the subsequent verse and acts in accordance with it.
This refers to the former.

Some versions read "I prostrate to all Buddhas" (namo sarvabuddhānām), but "joyfully praising" (xicheng) is correct. The standard term *namas* is also rendered as *namo*; this means "reverent salutation."
If one says "ban-tan" or "ban-di," this means "prostration"; the old term "he-nan" is a corruption and abbreviation thereof. The Sūtra states:
"Again, he formed this thought... up to: 'I too shall act in accordance [with it]'" (經「復作如是念至我亦隨順行」).
The commentary says:
"To contemplate and comply" refers to his practice.

Having encountered a favorable condition that exhorted him to employ provisional transformation, he contemplated that in order to bring forth beings in the turbid kalpa, he should comply with their ways.
Regarding the sutra passage, "Having reflected upon this matter, he went and taught it to the five bhikṣus," the commentary states:
The following three and a half verses correctly explain the transformation through the three vehicles, which is divided into three parts:

The first one and a half verses properly initiate the provisional transformation; the next verse brings about the emergence of the Three Jewels; and the final verse unifies the ancient and the present.
This is the first [section].
That which is called *Vārāṇasī* in Sanskrit is erroneously transcribed as *Bolanai*.
In the region of Central India, there were formerly two herds of deer, each numbering more than five hundred. The Buddha was the king of one herd, and Devadatta was likewise the king of the other.
At that time, as the king was hunting in the marshy plains, the Bodhisattva, the Deer King, went before him and entreated the king, saying:

"Great King, you pursue game in the central lands, releasing hunters and loosing flying arrows; thus all my followers will lose their lives this morning. Today they would rot and stink, providing nothing for your meal. I pray that you allow us to take turns, sending one deer each day; thus Your Majesty may have fresh meat for your cuisine, and I may prolong the lives of my kin for day and night."
The king approved of these words and turned his carriage back; the two herds of deer took turns in offering up their lives.
Within the herd of Deva, there was a pregnant doe whose turn had come to die. She said to her leader:
"Though my body should die, my offspring has not yet reached its turn."
"I pray that you will grant me leave for a short time; I shall go as soon as my child is born.
The Deer King said in anger, "Who does not cherish their own life?"
The female deer sighed and said, "Our king is unrighteous; his death is imminent.
She then hurriedly informed the Bodhisattva, and the Deer King, the Bodhisattva, said:
"How tragic! A compassionate mother’s heart extends its grace even to that which has not yet taken form; I shall now take your place.
Having reached the royal gate, the people along the road raised their voices in unison, crying out:
That great deer king has now come into the town,
and among the officials and commoners, there is none who does not rush to see him.
When the King heard of this, he considered it to be untrue.
The gatekeeper informed the king, and the king believed it to be so.
The king asked,
"Why has the deer king come so suddenly?"
The deer king said,
"There is a doe who is due to die, yet her fetus has not yet been born;
my heart cannot bear this, and I dare to offer my own body as a substitute."
Upon hearing this, the king sighed in admiration and said:
"I am one with a human body but the heart of a deer, lacking the mind of compassionate nurture;
you are one with a deer's body but the virtue of a man, possessing the merit of sacrificing your life for another."

Thereupon, he released all the deer and no longer required them to pay their lives as tribute; he immediately made that forest a sanctuary for the deer, and thus it was called the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), from which the name "Deer Forest" (Luyuan) originated.

His original name was *Sarvārthasiddha*, which in the Tang language means "Accomplisher of All Aims" (formerly called *Siddhārtha*, which is a corruption and abbreviation). After the Prince had transcended the city walls, he dwelt among mountains and hid in valleys, sacrificing his life to serve the Dharma. King Śuddhodana then commanded three members of the royal clan and two from the maternal side, saying:

"My son Sarvārthasiddha has renounced the household to pursue his studies; he wanders alone through mountains and marshes and dwells solitary in forests and thickets. Therefore, I command you all to follow him and learn where he stays."

Internally, there were paternal uncles and maternal uncles; externally, they were both sovereigns and subjects. In all their movements and stillness, they ought to have known when to advance and when to desist.
Five men bore their mandates and kept watch over one another as a protective guard; thus, they diligently sought a way to achieve liberation, frequently saying to one another:
"Now, those who cultivate the Way—do they realize it through suffering or through joy?"
The two said that ease is the way; the three said that diligent austerity is the way.

As these two groups disputed without being able to clarify the matter, the Prince contemplated the ultimate truth and, in order to subdue the non-Buddhist practitioners of asceticism, sustained his body with only hemp and wheat.
The two men saw him and said:
"The conduct of the Prince is not the true Dharma. Now, the Way is that which is realized through joy; since he now undergoes such toil and suffering, he is not one of our kind."
Abandoning [the practice], they fled far away to contemplate the realization of the fruit.

After the Prince had practiced austerities for six years without attaining Bodhi, he wished to verify that such asceticism was not the true path; thus, by accepting the milk-gruel, he realized the fruit. Hearing this, the three men sighed and said:
"His merit was on the verge of completion, yet now it has regressed; the fruits of six years of asceticism have been abandoned in a single day."
They also departed.
Thereupon, they went together to seek out the two men; having met them, they sat upright and engaged in high discourse, further deliberating among themselves:

"In the past, we saw Prince Sarvārthasiddha leave the royal palace for the wilderness, casting off precious garments to don deerskins, exerting himself with diligence and resolve, maintaining his integrity through bitter toil, seeking the profound and subtle Dharma in anticipation of the unsurpassed fruit. Now, however, he has accepted the milk-gruel from a cowherd’s daughter; we know that he has failed in the Way and compromised his resolve."
"It is of no avail.
The two men said, "Why did you see this so late? This is merely a man who has gone mad!"

Now, dwelling in the deep palace and abiding in the security of supreme honor, one cannot still the will to withdraw into the mountain forests; to renounce the rank of a Wheel-Turning King for the conduct of a lowly person—how could such a thing even be worth considering!
The term "zēngchěn" (增磣) means to increase one's revulsion.

When the Bodhisattva bathed in the Nairañjanā River and sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans. In tranquil stillness, he contemplated those who should be delivered and thought:
"That Udraka Rāmaputra has realized the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he is capable of receiving my Dharma."
The devas in the sky immediately replied to his voice, saying:
"It has been seven days since Udraka Rāmaputra passed away.
The Tathāgata sighed with regret:"
"Why have I not encountered him? Having heard the wondrous Dharma, he has suddenly passed away through transformation.
Let me observe further; there is Ārāḍa Kālāma, who has attained the meditative concentration of the sphere of nothingness and can transmit the ultimate truth."
The devas further said:
"Five days have already passed since his life ended;
the Tathāgata has repeatedly sighed in pity for his meager merit."
Furthermore, he carefully observed who should receive his instruction and saw that there were five people at the Deer Park (Ṛṣipatana) whom he could first guide.

At that time, the Tathāgata rose from beneath the Bodhi tree and proceeded toward the Deer Park; his deportment was serene and his divine radiance shone brilliantly. His majestic countenance possessed the luster of jade, and his body was as pure and bright as gold. He advanced with calm dignity to lead those five men.
When these five men saw the Tathāgata from afar, they said to one another:
"This is Sarvārthasiddha coming; though the years have passed swiftly, he has not realized the fruit of sainthood. His heart's desire having already turned back, he now seeks us out.
We should each remain silent and not rise to welcome or pay him homage."

As the Tathāgata drew near, his majestic spiritual power moved the five men; they forgot their self-restraint, rising to greet him with bows and inquiries after his well-being, attending upon him according to proper ritual.
The Tathāgata then gradually guided them, revealing to them the sublime principles.
The traditional interpretation explains that the "five people" are:
first, Cunda; second, Vīrya-Kāśyapa; [and so forth].
Third, Aśvajit—some say he was the bhikṣu Aśvajit;
fourth, Bhadrika;
fifth, Mahānāman Kauṇḍinya.
One should consult the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Why were there only five people?

Some say that during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were nine fellow students; four of them possessed sharp faculties and had already attained the Way previously, while these five possessed dull faculties and thus only now realized it, having made a vow to encounter the appearance of Śākyamuni Buddha and attain the Way.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "In the past, Śākyamuni took the form of a great fish and made a vow: 'Whoever eats me first shall be delivered first.
Because the five men ate him first, he delivered them first."

Furthermore, a sutra states: "Six people once made offerings to the Buddha; five took rice blossoms to offer, while one waited for them to ripen. Of these, five attained initial awakening while one remained behind—this was Subhadra."

Furthermore, it was these same five yakṣas who ate the flesh of King Maitrībala; among those five men, Cunda attained the first fruit [of the path], while the other four were at the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*), attaining the Way only at the beginning of the summer retreat.
The *Record of the Western Regions* states: "Only after completing the summer retreat did he attain the traces of the Path.

The dharma of the mark of cessation is precisely suchness (*tathatā*); it cannot be proclaimed through words because its nature is beyond verbal expression. Since dharmas are devoid of names and marks, they are explained by means of names and marks; this is the power of skillful means (*upāya*). Thus, he proceeded to Vārāṇasī to preach for the sake of the five men.
The Sūtra says: "This is called the turning of the Wheel of Dharma," up to "the distinct names of the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
The commentary states:
Thus, the Three Jewels have come into being.
The meaning of this wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) shall be briefly analyzed by way of five sections:
first, the determination of its essence; second, the explanation of its name; third, the characteristics of its turning; fourth, its classifications; and fifth, its relation to the three vehicles.

Regarding the definition of its essence, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter twenty-four, states: "That which is called the nature of a śramaṇa is also termed a brāhmaṇa and is also called the Brahma-wheel, because it is turned by the true Brahmā. Within this, only the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is designated as the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), because it resembles a wheel in terms of its swiftness and other qualities, or because it possesses spokes and other such parts."

In this context, the Blessed One has in some places designated the path of seeing (darśanamārga) as the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra). Just as a worldly wheel possesses characteristics such as speed and so forth, the path of seeing is called the Wheel of Dharma because it resembles that [worldly wheel].

It is said that because the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga) proceeds with great speed, involves acceptance and rejection, subdues what has not yet been subdued, pacifies what has already been subdued, and revolves between the higher and lower realms—it possesses these five similarities and is thus like a worldly wheel.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra* states:

"Just as the wheel of a noble king takes up what is ahead and leaves behind what is behind, so too is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); for it abandons objects such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and takes up [objects] such as origination (*samudaya*)."

This intention demonstrates that the vision of the principles of the Four Truths does not necessarily occur simultaneously; for instance, it is like the wheel of a Universal Monarch descending before [the territories] have been subdued. Thus spoke the Venerable Ghoṣaka.

Just as a worldly wheel possesses spokes and other components, the eight branches of the Noble Path resemble it and are thus called a "wheel. Specifically, right view, right intention, right effort, and right mindfulness resemble the spokes of a worldly wheel; right speech, right action, and right livelihood resemble the hub; and right concentration resembles the rim. Therefore, it is called the Wheel of Dharma.

How can it be known that the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) is exclusively the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), given that when the Path of Seeing arose for Kauṇḍinya and others, it was said that the True Wheel of Dharma had been turned?
The master Vasubandhu, relying on the Sautrāntika school, refutes the Sarvāstivāda by stating:
"The three turnings of the aspects (*ākāra*) are not exclusively the Path of Seeing; how then can this be asserted?"

The designation "Wheel of Dharma" (dharmacakra) is established only in reference to the Path of Seeing; therefore, it is only this very teaching consisting of the three turnings and twelve aspects that can logically be called the Wheel of Dharma.
What is meant by "turning"?
It is because through this dharma-gate, one proceeds to the mental continuum of another to cause them to understand the meaning.

Alternatively, all noble paths (āryamārga) are called the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), for they turn within the bodies of those to be converted; since the path of seeing (darśanamārga) has already reached its initial turning at the moment it arises in the continuum of another, it is said to have "already turned."

Regarding this, there is an interpretation which states that the initial teaching of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) is called the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra); however, this is not the correct tenet of the Sarvāstivāda. The *Abhidharmahṛdaya* also records an incorrect tenet, saying:
"The Muni taught that the Path of Seeing, because of its swiftness, is called the Wheel of Dharma."
The *Abhidharmakośa* further states:
"Alternatively, all noble paths (*āryamārga*) are the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), etc.";
this is the original intention of the Sautrāntika masters. Therefore, the *Vyākhyāyukti* says:

"The fundamental intention of the Vaibhāṣikas is that all noble paths (*āryamārga*) are collectively termed the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), because they encompass the three turnings and the three paths.

When the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises within the mental continuum of another, it is called 'already turned' because it has reached the beginning of the turning; it is not only the path of seeing that alone is named the Wheel of Dharma by means of the eight branches of the noble path, for the explanation of Ghoṣaka is not the correct meaning."
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:

"In the first turning of birth, one acquires the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*); in the second turning of birth, the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*); and in the third turning of birth, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).
Furthermore, there are no twelve aspects (*ākāra*); it consists solely of the single aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Now, the Mahāyāna universally penetrates all texts; there are five wheels of the Dharma:
first, the wheel of self-nature, which refers to the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas, right view, right knowledge, and so forth.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 95, states:

"Because it is constituted by dharmas such as right view, it is called the Wheel of Dharma; for it involves the three turnings for oneself and others, encompassing both the paths of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), as well as the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*)."
Because the noble eye of wisdom can destroy the afflictions, it is called a "wheel.
The *Abhidharmakośa* also states:

"All noble paths are called the Wheel of Dharma," or alternatively, its substance is taken to be solely the eight branches of the noble path, because they fully possess the meanings of the hub, the rim, and the spokes.
Right view and right intention are called the hub, for they are the root.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are called the spokes, for they exist because of the hub.
Right mindfulness, diligence, and concentration are called the "rim" because they encompass and sustain the others.

This differs from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), for although the distinct modes of cultivation of these eight members of the Noble Path exist within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), their essence actually extends through the other paths—namely, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Otherwise, the World-Honored One would not possess the Eightfold Noble Path [in those stages].

The second is the cause of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), which refers to the various teachings—such as those derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation—that are capable of producing the subsequent noble paths (*āryamārga*).

This is because the *Anantaparyāya Sūtra* includes it among its seventeen names as the "Wheel of Dharma," and because various sūtras and śāstras refer to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma as the "Wheel of Dharma."
The *Abhidharmakośa* also states:
"This very teaching of the three turnings and twelve aspects is called the Wheel of Dharma because it is a gateway of all dharmas.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also says: "The three cycles and twelve aspects are called the means for attaining what is to be attained."
"Because the preceding serves as the cause for the subsequent, and their combination constitutes the cause for the fruit, it is termed 'expedient means' (*upāya*).

Furthermore, it says: "The three cycles of the correct turning [of the wheel] correspond respectively to the stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning; the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) through wisdom and vision is termed 'expedient means.'"
The "three wheels of retinue" refers to the five aggregates that act as the companions to the noble paths.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state:

"The precepts cherished by the noble ones, as well as qualities such as faith, assist contemplation in becoming more luminous and assist the path in eliminating delusions; however, they are not the actual abandonments themselves."
The objects of the four wheels of Dharma refer to the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The objective referent for the sake of attaining what is to be attained refers to the Four Noble Truths."

This sutra also states that "Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū turned the twelve links of dependent origination," and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states that "by relying on the manifest characteristic (*vyakta-lakṣaṇa*), the teaching of the three natures as being all based upon the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is called the Wheel of Dharma."

Regarding the fruit of the five wheels of Dharma, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further states: "That which is to be attained is called Great Bodhi. Later in the text, it further states: "That which is subsumed under the four fruits of the śramaṇa—namely, the enlightenment of śrāvakas, the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas, and the unsurpassed enlightenment of all Tathāgatas—is the fruit of the Dharma-discourse."

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further states: "The three cycles of twelve aspects are called the means for attaining what is to be attained. It also says: "When the three cycles proceed correctly, the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of knowledge and vision—corresponding respectively to the stages of seeing (*darśana*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)—are called the means of attainment; therefore, enlightenment (*bodhi*) and nirvāṇa are called the fruits to be attained."
However, these five bodies do not exceed four categories:
first, the teaching; second, the principle; third, the practice; and fourth, the fruit.
To explain their names:
First, it is called the "Brahma-wheel" (*brahma-cakra*); since the Tathāgata, the Arhat, is a synonym for Brahmā, and because he sets this wheel in motion, it is also called the Brahma-wheel.

Second, it is called the "Dharma-wheel" (*dharma-cakra*); "Dharma" carries the meaning of that which is to be followed and maintained, and because it is constituted by the dharmas such as right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), it is designated as the Dharma-wheel.
The wheel has four meanings:

first, the meaning of being complete, as it possesses a hub, a rim, and spokes; alternatively, when its essence and function—such as the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena—are fully provided, it is called a wheel.

Second is the meaning of "crushing and destroying": because these four kinds of dharmas—whether by subduing, severing, assisting, or correcting—are all capable of crushing those afflictions that have not yet been severed.
Third is the meaning of "subduing" (*viniyanti*): because the afflictions have already been subdued and their power rendered remote.

Fourth is the meaning of "not fixed" (*aniyata*): from one's own view to one's own cultivation; from one's own cultivation to one's own state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); from the wisdom of one's own state of no-more-learning, one utters words of instruction; others understand the principle of the Truths through these words of instruction; others give rise to right practice based on the principle of the Truths; others give rise to the wisdom of the fruit based on right practice;

and thus, through this successive progression, one further speaks it for others. This is like the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) possessed by a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*): because it can subdue those afflictions not yet subdued, it can suppress those afflictions already subdued, and because it moves back and forth.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "It should be understood that the Blessed One transferred the Dharma he had realized into the person of Ājñātakauṇḍinya; this was then transferred into the persons of others in succession, and those in turn transferred it into the persons of yet others. Because of this meaning of successive transfer, it is called a 'wheel' (*cakra*)."
The Dharma is itself the wheel; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
"To turn" (*vartana*) means to move, to manifest, to transport, or to give rise to.

It moves by proclaiming the teachings and manifests by extolling the sublime principles; it transports the Noble Path prior to words and gives rise to true wisdom subsequent to speech. To perfectly crush hindrances and afflictions is called "turning the wheel of the Dharma. Whether one takes "that which is turned" to be the wheel of Dharma, or "the turning of the wheel of Dharma," both explanations are valid.

Regarding the "turning of the wheel": when it is said that the turning of the wheel of Dharma occurs through nine and five aspects, one should know that this is called the "skillful turning of the wheel of Dharma.
First, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, he attained the objective sphere to be attained;
second, he attained the skillful means for that attainment.
Third, realizing that which one ought to realize for oneself;
fourth, having realized it, establishing it within the mental continuums of others so that they develop deep faith and understanding in one's own realization;
and fifth, causing others to develop deep faith and understanding in what has been realized.

This intent summarizes the manifestations of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) and its characteristics; it means that at the time of one’s own realization of the fruit, even śrāvakas and others are enabled to have their own realization. This does not rely on the principle of being established through the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) of a bodhisattva, nor does it rely on the principle of the transformation of an actual bodhisattva. Rather, the treatise is composed based on the entirety of the beginning, middle, and end, and does not rely on the attainment of the three turnings within a single assembly.

Regarding the objective referent (*ālambana-viṣaya*): it refers to the Four Noble Truths, which are subsumed under both the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) and the non-established truths (*avyavasthāna-satya*), as these depend upon the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Regarding the attainment of the skillful means (*upāya-pratilambha*): it refers to the twelvefold wisdom (*dvādaśākāra-jñāna*) that correctly revolves three times within these very Four Noble Truths; this constitutes the characteristic of the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma, serving as the cause for attaining unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*).

Regarding the "initial turning": this refers to when a bodhisattva in the past entered clear observation (*abhisamaya*) and, in accordance with reality, understood: "This is the noble truth of suffering," and so on, up to "this is the noble truth of the path. Within that process, whatever noble direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) is capable of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing is, at that time, called the "true noble eye of wisdom."

Precisely because these [three] differ according to whether they pertain to the past, future, or present, they are respectively termed knowledge (*jñāna*), clarity (*vidyā*), and awakening (*buddhi*).

This explains that a single wisdom is collectively named the "Dharma-eye" (*dharmacakṣus*), which possesses three modes of activity termed knowledge, clarity, and awakening; it does not mean that four distinct wisdoms arise separately regarding a single truth. Since the Path of True Seeing (*darśanamārga*) lasts for only a single moment, it differs from the gradual, sequential observation of the lower and upper realms found in the Hīnayāna. While it is said to "pervade the three times" based on the realization of cessation through its expression, this does not mean that the Truth of Cessation itself exists throughout the three times.

The second turning refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*), who, through their sublime wisdom, realize things as they truly are: "I still have further tasks to perform; I must fully comprehend the Truth of Suffering not yet known, I must permanently abandon the Truth of Origination not yet abandoned, I must realize the Truth of Cessation not yet realized, and I must cultivate the Truth of the Path not yet cultivated. Thus, there are likewise four aspects of practice, which should be understood as previously described.

The third turning refers to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who, having attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), declare: "That which was to be done has all been done by me. This means: "I have fully known the Truth of Suffering that was previously unknown," and so forth, as explained at length; likewise, "I have cultivated the Truth of the Path that was previously uncultivated," which should also be understood to have four aspects similar to the preceding.

As for this distinction: the four modes of activity of the first two turnings constitute the true noble eye of wisdom of those still in training (śaikṣa), while the final one constitutes the true noble eye of wisdom of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Examining the intent of this passage: at the time of the initial turning, during the stage of preparatory knowledge prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), although one knows the Four Truths, this is merely the cause for the turning and not yet the actual turning itself, because [the afflictions] have not yet been destroyed. For this reason, it is designated as "weakening power and augmenting capacity," and is subsumed under the category of the stage of turning.

Upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the true path of uninterrupted transition (*anantaryamārga*) is properly termed "the turning" (*parivṛtti*), because it directly abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Its corresponding path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and the path of seeing through characteristics (*lakṣaṇadarśanamārga*) are also termed the "initial turning," even though they do not abandon the afflictions; this is because they eliminate the heavy residues (*dausthulya*), consolidate what has already been suppressed, and likewise do not involve the distinct cognition of the characteristics of the Four Truths.

Subsequently, prior to the abandonment of afflictions while practicing the path, the activities that arise in association with thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) and so forth constitute the characteristic of "correct turning" (*samyak-parivṛtti*). This includes the correct arising of true wisdom up to the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), as well as the abandonment of all afflictions, which are likewise subsumed under this turning. Even the arising of distinct modes of activity that merely intend to proceed toward the noble state is included, because both the path of suppressing and the path of definitive abandonment are termed "turning."

Upon reaching the path of liberation of the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), one gives rise to the knowledge that "what was to be done has been done"; thereafter, there is nothing further to be severed, but only that which was previously suppressed remains subdued, with nothing yet unsubdued.

However, although there are paths of suppression prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are not designated as "turnings" because they are not untainted (*anāsrava*); since there is no untainted state prior [to the path of seeing], they differ from the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Thus, for the Bodhisattva himself, there are three turnings:

the first turning occurs in the path of seeing and is called the "turning of the seal of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇamudrāvarta*); the second turning occurs in the path of cultivation and is called the "turning of what is to be cultivated" (*bhāvyavarta*); the third turning occurs in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) and is called the "turning of what has been done" (*kṛtavarta*). At each turning, four aspects (*ākāra*) arise with respect to each Truth (*satya*). When these three turnings are discussed vertically, they constitute twelve aspects; thus, the four truths combined comprise forty-eight aspects.
